Initially, during Ramchandra Ray's escape, Udayaditya (the Yubaraj/prince) gave orders that Sitaram (the guard) obeyed, opening locked doors for him. Later, after Udayaditya is trapped in his own prison room due to a fire, Sitaram reverses the dynamic by taking the initiative to rescue him from the burning room, pulling him out to safety instead of waiting to follow commands from the prince.

Pratapaditya's initial failed plan was to order two Pathan men to intercept and kill Basanta Ray at the inn in Simultali on his way to Jessore. The method that finally succeeds in ending the old king's life is when Muktiyar Khan presents a signed death order to Basanta Ray; after being seized by soldiers, an Abdul stabs Basanta Ray with a bloodied sword during his prayers.

The Maharaj gets married today, so Vibha cannot enter the royal palace, and her hopes of happiness vanish like a mirage.

Rukmini's signet ring had a seal engraved with the Yubaraj's name. Sitaram and Bhagavat used this ring to stamp a forged petition claiming the Yubaraj lodged a treason complaint against Pratapaditya. Pratapaditya later presented this forged petition—bearing the Yubaraj's name from the ring's seal—as evidence to justify Udayaditya's imprisonment.

The midnight escape woke Pratapaditya and left the guards absent, waking his vigilance so he paid closer attention to Udayaditya. When Udayaditya secretly arranged a monthly stipend for the dismissed guards, Pratapaditya heard and became furious at this unauthorized act of dealing with commoners. To punish Udayaditya for his independent behavior, the king decreed that Surma must be exiled. Furthermore, Surma resigned herself to leaving because she worried that the guards would starve without Udayaditya's help, and she believed he would not assist them again given the new decree.

The emotional significance of the song is expressing profound loneliness, mourning the absence of loved ones, and the stark reality of being the sole survivor in a silent, empty household. Basanta Ray sings it in two contrasting contexts: first, alone on the veranda of his palace in Raigarh gazing at the setting sun, grieving the departure of his family and the broken sitar; and second, following the tragic news of Dada’s imprisonment and discovering Vibha alone in the silent room, where he takes her hand to soothe his solitude and find peace in his surviving family member.

Rukmini's failure to stop Udayaditya's escape allowed him to flee Raigarh. Since the Maharaja believed Udayaditya was dead in the fire, he became suspicious that Basanta Ray had helped him escape and ordered his death sentence, resulting in Basanta Ray's execution.

Pratapaditya initially received Ramchandra coldly and formally, showing no warmth or hospitality and treating him only as a royal guest to conduct business. In contrast, Ramchandra later attacked Pratapaditya's status with contempt, mocking him daily in court by comparing him to a leech/earthworm and openly expressing his own superior status over him.

She secretly returns to the palace during a storm while Udayaditya is holding a sleeping girl. Using her charm and tricks, she makes him remember their past, breaking his heart regarding Surma and causing him to abandon the child, which leads to his tragic anguish.

After returning to Jessore as a prisoner, Udayaditya asserts his unworthiness to his father. Following his father's declaration that he is not worthy, he formally renounces the throne by swearing an oath on Ma-Kali's feet, pledging that Samaraditya will be the heir and that he will never accept even an iota of the kingdom's land. Satisfied with the oath, his father agrees to grant him release.

The old Nayanchand intercepts the letter because he fears the Maharaj; he hands it to the Mahishi instead of delivering it to Jessore. To misrepresent the letter, the Mahishi tells the Maharaj that Ramchandra wrote it merely out of anger at them, and instructs Basanta Ray to announce in the household that Ramchandra wrote the letter requesting Vibha be sent back to her father-in-law’s house. This way, Vibha believes Ramchandra has forgiven her and wants her return, rather than discovering he renounced her.

Pratapaditya's attempt to trap Ramchandra Ray by blocking the canal with large Sal wood logs fails because the guards are unable to stop the escaping boat: their thrown stones do not reach it, and they lack gunpowder and bullets for the found gun. Furthermore, Ramchandra's men are able to pull the boat up and over the logs, clearing the path and escaping.

Basanta Ray's growing despair over Udayaditya's situation reflects in his relationship with the sitar because the instrument served as his eternal companion. When he is forced to leave, his grief hinders his playing, leading him to abandon the sitar and declare he will "not play it anymore." Later, after learning of Udayaditya's imprisonment, his overwhelming despair affects the sitar further by breaking its strings, rendering it unable to provide the comfort it once did.

Udayaditya's willingness to intervene on behalf of his oppressed subjects has completely disappeared. Before Surma's death, he would have intervened without consideration to stop an oppressive official and assist the subjects. After her death, his former courage was gone; he hesitates in every task, doubts every matter, and flees from seeing oppression, such as running into his house when he sees an official beating a subject, rather than stopping it. He also no longer has the courage to secretly help the oppressed subjects.

He used his staff as a rope tied to a pillar on the roof to lower the Maharaj onto his boat, and he physically lifted the unconscious Vibha into a palanquin to bring her out of the palace.

In Jessore, Vibha is heavily adorned by the Mahishi with eight thick gold bangles and diamond bracelets on both arms, a large nose ring, and an elaborate hairstyle, and is treated with affection as a princess. In Chandradwip, she radically shifts to being dressed as a common woman or maidservant, shedding these adornments and appearing exposed with a fallen veil. This stripped presentation demotes her to a beggar seeking alms, treating her as a lowly, unwelcomed servant rather than a royal figure.

In the bedchamber, the window symbolized his lingering comfort and hope regarding Surma's presence, representing the spot where she used to sit and from which he awaited her return, though often unfulfilled. In the prison cell, the window symbolizes the stark contrast between the view of freedom (sky, birds) and the surrounding darkness, representing a hopeful yet limited vision of eventual escape rather than Surma's comforting presence. It also marks the boundary where Vibha sees him as naturally free despite his imprisonment.

Initially, the dynamic was a flirtatious financial arrangement where Rukmini lent money to Sitaram for his living expenses, engaging in witty banter and playful teasing over the loan. After Udayaditya's imprisonment, Rukmini asserted power by reminding Sitaram that the Yubaraj was hers, blocking him from helping. This escalated when Sitaram arranged for Udayaditya's prison cell to be set ablaze to kill him. Upon returning, Sitaram found Rukmini hostile, and she threatened his life, stating she would lay him and the Yubaraj in an oven. Fleeing in terror, Sitaram later returned to seek revenge; at that point, Rukmini incited the guards to punish him, transforming their relationship into a life-threatening enmity where she held the power to destroy him.

Sitaram first creates a chaotic diversion using fires and alarm to draw the guards' attention away, allowing Udayaditya to escape. To cover up the escape, Sitaram then intentionally burns his own empty prison cell, causing a collapse and shouts that divert attention from the guardhouse, destroys physical evidence (throwing the sword and bones inside), and fabricates a story that Udayaditya died in the fire. By fleeing the city himself while leaving the false death rumor intact, Sitaram ensures the king will not suspect Udayaditya's escape.

Ramchandra Ray interpreted Udayaditya's actions as inevitable and expected, believing that if his life were in peril, others would also unite to save him, and their troubles would not matter. Furthermore, he believed Udayaditya had saved him solely for the sake of his sister, meaning he did not feel genuine gratitude toward him. Consequently, Ramchandra Ray made fun of Udayaditya in court rather than acknowledging the rescue.

A forged petition is created stating that the Prince Udayaditya lodged a treason complaint against his father with the Emperor of Delhi. Upon hearing this news, Pratapaditya relies on the political specter of the Emperor's wrath rather than investigating the source of the complaint, ultimately using this fear as the mechanism to imprison his son.

Vibha's hair serves as a marker of Surma's presence and subsequent tragic absence because she secretly goes to Surma to have her hair styled to her liking, showing her deep dependence on Surma's touch. Later, she waits daily for Surma to braid her hair to soothe her grief, but when Surma is absent, her hair remains unbraided, marking both her reliance on Surma and the tragic reality of Surma's absence and the depth of Vibha's sorrow.
